business_summary: Sagility is a business services company. It grew sales at a 19.47% three-year CAGR to FY26, with an operating margin of 24.53% and low borrowings (debt/equity 0.11x). Net profit was Rs 924.77 cr in FY26 and Rs 1026.41 cr over the last four quarters. The evidence does not describe its operations.
why_own: The case rests on steady double-digit revenue growth at a stable, high operating margin, with profit backed by cash and little debt. Evidence is thin: no supplied documents, no 5-year growth figure and no comparison of valuation with its own history, so the drivers are metric-only and the reason profit has grown much faster than sales is untested.

drivers.statement: Revenue keeps compounding at a double-digit rate (3-year CAGR currently 19.47%).
Operating margin holds near its current 24.53% level; it was essentially unchanged over three years (-0.1 pp).
Reported profit is backed by cash: operating cash flow is 1.3x net profit. (warn line tightened by code from 0.9 to 0.91.)
The balance sheet stays conservative, with debt/equity at 0.11x and interest cover at 13.49x. (warn line tightened by code from 0.4 to 0.14.)

kill_criteria.description: Operating margin falls below 17%, well below the current 24.53%.
Three-year revenue CAGR falls below 8%, which would end the growth case.

risks.statement: Net profit 3-year CAGR is 86.06% against revenue growth of 19.47%, with margin flat over the same period. The evidence does not explain this gap, so the sustainability of profit growth is untested.
Returns on capital are modest (ROCE 12.42%, ROE 10.28%) for a stock at 20.74x trailing earnings and 2.2x book. No comparison with its own valuation history is available.
The record is short: the 5-year revenue CAGR is not available, so the durability of growth is less proven.

skeptic_counter_case: The thesis could be wrong if the 86% three-year profit CAGR came from items below the operating line (lower interest, depreciation or tax, or a depressed starting base) rather than repeatable operations. Revenue grew 19.47% and operating margin was flat (-0.1 pp), so operations alone cannot explain that gap. If profit growth reverts toward revenue growth, a 20.74x trailing P/E on a 12.42% ROCE and 10.28% ROE looks expensive. The monitoring thresholds are also loose: margin must fall about 7.5 pp to 17% before a kill, and growth must fall below 8%. Deterioration could go unflagged for a long time. The evidence is thin, so this is a challenge, not a proof. What would change this view: A breakdown showing that the FY23-FY26 profit growth came from operating drivers that continue (not one-off or below-the-line items or a depressed base), together with a P/E that is not above this stock's own 5-year median.
